implementation_notes: The whole structure is a library: flyweight<T> is a pointer-sized handle whose associated value lives once in a factory owned by the instantiation; hashed_factory does hashed lookup, refcounted tracking erases the entry when the last handle dies, and key_value<Key, Value> avoids constructing the costly value when an equivalent entry already exists. Flyweights are not mutable - assignment rebinds the handle - and the extrinsic state stays in your own objects. Choose this variant when Boost is available: tracking, locking and storage policies are all configurable, which the hand-written pool cannot offer.
pitfalls: flyweight<T> is immutable: a method that wants to change the value must assign a new one, and by_key_value construction can be far more expensive than a lookup if the key type is not separated from the value.
Construction performs a hash lookup plus a mutex-protected insert, so it is measurably slower than constructing a plain T; use no_tracking when the pool may live as long as the process.

The default static_holder makes the factory a function-local static, which brings destruction-order and shared-library surprises; multi-threaded interning needs concurrent_factory or an appropriate locking policy.

variants.name: Standard-library pool (unordered_map to shared_ptr<const T>)
variants.implementation_notes: Without Boost the factory is a few lines over the standard library: an unordered_map from a stable key to shared_ptr<const T> returns the canonical instance, and const in the handle makes the intrinsic state immutable by type while the last owner frees the entry. Use string_view keys with a transparent hash (C++20 heterogeneous lookup) or a string_view-keyed map to avoid building keys on lookup, and std::pmr if the values should live in a monotonic arena. What it lacks relative to Boost.Flyweight is the policy layer: eviction, tracking and synchronization are yours to design.
pitfalls: The map holds the last reference forever unless entries are erased: a pool keyed on unbounded input is a leak. Erase on the last use or key it weakly.
Concurrent insertion needs a mutex (or a sharded map) and a second check after locking, otherwise two threads create two 'canonical' instances for one key.
std::string_view keys are safe only while the underlying storage outlives the pool; with a string-keyed map the lookup allocates, which can dominate a hot path.
